# Lao sticky rice (khao niao)

Sticky rice soaked, steamed and kept warm in a covered basket, then pinched off and rolled into small balls by children's own hands. In Laos and in Lao homes everywhere, sticky rice is shared from one basket and eaten with the fingers.

## Makes enough for

6 children

## Ingredients

- 2 cups sticky rice (also sold as glutinous or sweet rice)
- cool water for rinsing and soaking
- 1 small cucumber, if we like

## Tools

- a large bowl for soaking
- a strainer
- a bamboo sticky rice basket (huad) and its pot, or a steamer basket lined with a damp cloth
- an induction hot plate
- a lid or a damp cloth to cover the rice
- a large tray or shallow bowl
- a rice paddle or flat wooden spoon
- a covered rice basket (tip khao) or a bowl with a damp cloth
- a small bowl of water for wetting hands
- one child knife and cutting board for each child who is cutting
- measuring cups
- a plate for each child

## Steps

- Wash our hands with soap and water.
- Measure the rice into the large bowl and rinse it in cool water, swishing with our hands, until the water runs almost clear.
- Cover the rice with plenty of cool water and let it soak for at least 4 hours, or overnight.
- Pour the rice into the strainer and let it drain.
- An adult puts a few inches of water in the pot and brings it to a boil.
- Spoon the rice into the steamer basket.
- An adult sets the basket over the boiling water and covers the rice.
- Steam the rice for about 15 minutes, until the grains on top look shiny.
- An adult flips the rice over in one piece and steams it about 10 minutes more, until every grain is soft and see-through.
- An adult turns the rice out onto the tray and spreads it with the paddle to let the steam out.
- Gather the rice into the covered basket to keep it warm and soft.
- Wash the cucumber under running water.
- Cut the cucumber into sticks with child knives.
- Wash our hands well again, since everyone touches the food.
- Dip our fingers in the bowl of water.
- Pinch off a small piece of rice and roll it in our palm into a little ball.
- Eat it with our fingers, with a cucumber stick alongside.

## Why we use it

Rolling a small ball of warm sticky rice in one palm builds hand strength (fine motor development). Children watch the rice change through soaking and steaming. Eating from a shared basket with our hands lets children eat sticky rice the way it is eaten in Lao homes. Sticky rice has no gluten, even though it is sometimes called glutinous rice.

## I wonder

- I wonder why this rice sticks together when other rice falls apart.
- I wonder what happens to the rice grains while they soak.
- I wonder how steam can cook food.

## Connections

- Children can compare a few dry grains with soaked grains and steamed grains.
- The cloudy rinse and soaking water goes on a garden bed.
- Cucumbers come from our summer beds and the weekly produce bin.

## Cutting for our youngest

- Cucumber is a soft first food for child knives. Children cut sticks with an adult close beside each child who is cutting (close supervision). The others can rinse rice or fill the water bowl.
- Children wait until the rice is cool enough to touch before they roll it.
- Children eat sitting down with an adult nearby.

## Clean up

- Rinse water goes on a garden bed.
- Children scrape the stuck rice off their hands into the compost and wash their hands.
- Cucumber ends go to the compost.
- Child knives. Washed one at a time, never left in a sink of water, dried and returned to the knife roll with the blades covered.
- Cutting boards. Scrubbed with hot soapy water, rinsed, sanitized and stood upright to dry.
- Bowl, strainer and measuring cups. Children may wash and dry them. The educator rewashes as needed.
- Steamer basket. Rinsed with cool water, scrubbed of stuck grains and left to air dry fully.
- Pot, tray and rice paddle. Washed and dried by the educator.
- Induction hot plate. Cooled, surface wiped.
- Children sweep their own space with the dustpan and brush. The educator finishes and checks each tool before it is put away.
